title: The Congo: A Land Cursed by Wealth
citation: Dan Snow, The Congo: A Land Cursed by Wealth, BBC News Website, 2013
paragraphs: The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is often described as a paradox—a nation with the natural wealth to become one of the richest countries on earth, yet ranked among the poorest. Its history is a grim story of exploitation, violence, and corruption, shaped by centuries of colonialism and foreign interference.

The DRC has endured the world’s deadliest conflict since 1945, with more than five million people killed and millions more suffering displacement, disease, violence and famine. This devastating reality, sometimes called “Africa’s Great War,” has been fought largely within Congo’s borders, fueled by the fight to control its immense resources.

Ironically, it is these resources that lie at the heart of the country’s suffering. From the Portuguese slave trade of the 15th century to King Leopold of Belgium’s rubber empire in the 19th century, foreign powers have plundered Congo’s people and land. Millions died as men were enslaved to tap rubber, their families held hostage, resistance punished by mutilation and murder. Later, Congo’s copper, uranium, and coltan helped fuel world wars and the digital revolution—yet the Congolese themselves remained impoverished and uneducated, denied the chance to build stable institutions.

Independence in 1960 brought hope, but no preparation. With no trained elite to govern, chaos followed. The Cold War further destabilized the nation, with Western powers propping up dictator Mobutu Sese Seko, who looted billions while his people starved. His fall in 1997 triggered another brutal war, drawing in nine nations and countless militias. Today, Congo remains fractured. Its minerals still flow abroad, enriching elites and global industries, while its people endure poverty and instability. The Congo’s tragedy is not its weakness but its wealth—a blessing turned into a curse by centuries of exploitation.
